lessons.title: Types of Sprinklers: Impact, Rotor, and Micro-Sprinklers
lessons.body:
Sprinklers are a practical way to water small farms, but choosing the right type matters. Impact sprinklers, also called hammer sprinklers, are the classic metal ones that go 'chk-chk-chk' as they rotate. They are tough, cheap, and work well with dirty water. A common model is the 1/2-inch brass impact sprinkler that covers a 10-12 meter radius at 2-3 bar pressure. They are ideal for field crops like maize, beans, and vegetables. However, they need higher pressure and can be knocked over by wind.

Rotor sprinklers use a gear-driven mechanism to rotate smoothly. They are quieter and more uniform than impact types. A typical plastic rotor sprinkler covers 8-12 meters and operates at 1.5-3 bar. They are great for small plots and orchards because you can adjust the spray pattern. But they are more sensitive to dirty water and may clog if you use pond water without a filter.

Micro-sprinklers, also called micro-sprays or mini-sprinklers, are small plastic devices that spray a fine mist or low-angle jet. They cover 1-3 meters and work at low pressure (0.5-1.5 bar). They are perfect for seedbeds, nurseries, and closely spaced crops like spinach and onions. They use less water but require clean water and frequent cleaning. They are not suitable for tall crops because the spray is low.

For a small farm in Africa, start with impact sprinklers if you have a strong pump and dirty water. Use rotors if you want even coverage and have filtered water. Use micro-sprinklers for delicate crops and small areas. Always check the manufacturerâs recommended pressure and spacing. A mix of types can work: impact for field edges, micro for seedbeds. Remember, the best sprinkler is the one that fits your water source, crop, and budget.

lessons.title: Designing a Portable Sprinkler System
lessons.body:
A portable sprinkler system lets you move pipes and sprinklers from one block to another, saving money on pipes. Start by measuring your plot. Suppose you have a 20m x 30m vegetable garden. You want to cover it with sprinklers spaced 12m apart. You will need a mainline pipe (usually 32mm or 40mm HDPE) and lateral pipes (20mm or 25mm) that carry water to sprinklers.

First, find your water source. A small pump that delivers 50-100 liters per minute at 2-3 bar is typical. Check the pump curve or test with a pressure gauge. Next, plan the layout. For a rectangular plot, run the mainline along one side. Then connect lateral pipes at intervals equal to sprinkler spacing. Use quick-connect couplers so you can move laterals easily. Each lateral can have 2-4 sprinklers, depending on pressure and pipe size.

Calculate the total flow needed. If each impact sprinkler uses 10 liters per minute (L/min), and you have 6 sprinklers, you need 60 L/min. Ensure your pump can supply that at the required pressure. If not, reduce the number of sprinklers per lateral or use smaller nozzles. Also, consider pipe friction loss: for every 10 meters of 20mm pipe, you lose about 0.2 bar. So keep laterals short (under 30m) or use larger pipe.

Use a filter if your water is dirty. A simple screen filter (mesh 80-120) will protect sprinklers. Place it after the pump. Add a valve at each lateral to control flow. For portability, use pipes with quick couplers and store them on a reel or rack. Mark sprinkler positions with stakes so you can move the system quickly. Always flush pipes before connecting sprinklers to remove debris. With a well-designed portable system, two people can move and set up a 20x30m plot in 30 minutes.

lessons.title: Calculating Sprinkler Spacing and Application Rates
lessons.body:
Getting spacing and application rates right saves water and ensures even coverage. Sprinkler spacing depends on the sprinklerâs wetted diameter. For an impact sprinkler with a 12m radius (24m diameter), you should space them at 60% of diameter, so 14-15 meters apart. For rotors with 10m radius (20m diameter), space at 12 meters. Micro-sprinklers with 2m radius (4m diameter) are spaced 2-3 meters apart. Always overlap sprinkler patterns by at least 30% to avoid dry spots.

Application rate is how fast water is applied, measured in millimeters per hour (mm/hr). If your sprinkler delivers 10 L/min over a 12m x 12m square (144 mÂ²), that is 10 L/min = 600 L/hr. 600 L over 144 mÂ² = 4.17 mm/hr. Most soils can absorb 5-10 mm/hr. If your rate is higher, you get runoff. To reduce rate, use smaller nozzles or space sprinklers further apart.

To calculate how long to run, first find your crop water need. In dry season, vegetables need about 5 mm/day. If your application rate is 4 mm/hr, you need 5/4 = 1.25 hours (75 minutes) per day. But you don't water every day if you apply more. For example, if you water every 3 days, you need 15 mm per session, so 15/4 = 3.75 hours. Use a rain gauge or tin cans to check actual application. Place 5-10 cans around the plot, run the system for 30 minutes, and measure average depth. Adjust run time accordingly.

Remember, wind affects uniformity. In windy conditions, reduce spacing or run at night. Also, pressure changes affect flow: if pressure drops, application rate drops. Use a pressure gauge at the sprinkler to confirm. Keep a simple log of run times and rainfall to avoid over- or under-watering. With practice, you can fine-tune spacing and timing to match your soil and crop.

lessons.title: Setting Up and Moving Sprinklers Efficiently
lessons.body:
Moving sprinklers by hand is hard work, but with a system you can do it quickly. First, lay out your mainline and laterals in a pattern that lets you move in one direction. For example, start at one corner and work across the field. Use quick-connect couplers (like Camlock or Gardena) so you can snap pipes together without tools. Keep a few spare couplers and gaskets in your pocket.

Before you start, check that all sprinklers are clean and nozzles are the right size. Set up the first lateral, turn on the pump, and check for leaks. Walk along the line and listen for hissing or see if water sprays unevenly. Fix leaks by tightening couplers or replacing gaskets. Once the first block is watered (say, 1 hour), turn off the pump, wait 2 minutes for pressure to drop, then disconnect the lateral. Move the whole lateral to the next position. If you have multiple laterals, you can move them one by one while others are running, but ensure the pump can handle the flow.

To save time, use a 'two-line' system: one lateral is watering while you set up the next. This keeps water application continuous. For a 20x30m plot, you might have three positions per lateral. With two people, you can move a 30m lateral in 5 minutes. Always drag pipes, don't lift them, to avoid damage. Use a pipe hook or a simple Y-shaped stick to lift and carry.

At the end of the day, drain pipes if frost is possible (rare in most of Africa, but highlands can get cold). Store pipes on a rack or reel to prevent kinks. Mark sprinkler positions with bright stakes so you don't lose time measuring. Train a helper: one person operates the pump, the other moves pipes. Set a rhythm: water, move, water, move. With practice, you can cover a hectare in a day with a portable system.

lessons.title: Winterizing and Storing Sprinkler Equipment
lessons.body:
In most of Africa, winter means a dry season, not freezing. But in highland areas like Kenyaâs Rift Valley or Ethiopiaâs highlands, temperatures can drop below freezing at night. Even if you donât have frost, proper storage extends equipment life. After the last irrigation, drain all water from pipes, sprinklers, and pump. Water left in pipes can freeze and burst them, or cause rust and algae.

Start by turning off the pump and opening all drain valves. If your pipes donât have drains, disconnect them and tilt to let water out. Remove sprinklers and shake out water. For impact sprinklers, unscrew the nozzle and let it dry. For rotors, remove the cap and drain. Micro-sprinklers can be soaked in a vinegar solution (1 part vinegar to 4 parts water) for 30 minutes to dissolve mineral deposits, then rinse and dry.

Clean all filters. A screen filter can be rinsed with a hose. If you have a sand filter, backwash it. Store pipes in a shaded, dry place. UV light degrades plastic, so keep them out of direct sun. Hang pipes vertically or lay them flat on a rack, not on the ground where termites or rodents can chew them. Coil flexible pipes loosely; tight coils can cause kinks. Store sprinklers in a bucket or box, not on the ground.

Lubricate metal parts: put a few drops of oil on impact sprinkler bearings and rotor gears. Check O-rings and gaskets; replace any that are cracked. For the pump, drain fuel and oil, or run it dry if itâs electric. Store the pump in a dry place. Make an inventory: count sprinklers, couplers, and pipes. Note any repairs needed for next season. A well-stored system can last 5-10 years. In areas with no frost, you can skip draining if you run the system weekly, but if you leave it idle for months, drain it. Always store away from children and livestock.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting Common Sprinkler Problems
lessons.body:
Sprinklers can fail in many ways. The most common problem is uneven coverage: some areas get too much water, others too little. First, check pressure. If pressure is low, sprinklers wonât rotate or spray far. Use a pressure gauge at the sprinkler. Most impact sprinklers need 2-3 bar. If pressure is below 1.5 bar, check for clogged filters, closed valves, or a worn pump impeller. Clean the filter and open all valves. If pressure is still low, you may have too many sprinklers on one line. Reduce the number or use larger pipe.

If a sprinkler doesnât rotate, the bearing may be dirty or damaged. For impact sprinklers, remove the body and clean the bearing with a brush and water. Apply a drop of oil. For rotors, remove the cap and rinse the gear. If the sprinkler sprays but doesnât turn, the nozzle may be too large for the pressure. Try a smaller nozzle. Also, check for debris in the nozzle: unscrew it and poke with a wire.

Leaks at couplers are common. Replace worn gaskets or O-rings. If a pipe cracks, cut out the damaged section and join with a repair coupling. For a quick fix, wrap with self-amalgamating tape. If water sprays from the base of a sprinkler, the seal is bad; replace it. If the pump loses prime, check for air leaks on the suction side. Tighten all connections and ensure the suction hose is not blocked.

If you see dry spots, your spacing may be too wide or wind is blowing the spray. Reduce spacing or run at night. If runoff occurs, your application rate is too high. Use smaller nozzles or pulse the system (run 15 minutes on, 15 off). Keep a simple toolkit: spare nozzles, gaskets, wire, and a pressure gauge. Most problems are solved by cleaning, tightening, or replacing a small part. If you canât fix it, ask a neighbor or extension officer. Regular maintenance prevents most breakdowns.

quiz.q: Which type of sprinkler is best for dirty water and high pressure?
quiz.explanation: Impact sprinklers are durable and handle dirty water better than rotors or micro-sprinklers.

quiz.q: What is a typical wetted radius for a micro-sprinkler?
quiz.explanation: Micro-sprinklers are small and cover a radius of 1-3 meters.

quiz.q: Which sprinkler type operates at the lowest pressure?
quiz.explanation: Micro-sprinklers work at 0.5-1.5 bar, lower than impact or rotor sprinklers.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for an impact sprinkler with a 12m radius?
quiz.explanation: Space at 60% of wetted diameter (24m), so about 14-15 meters.

quiz.q: If a sprinkler delivers 10 L/min over 144 mÂ², what is the application rate?
How much water do vegetables typically need per day in dry season?
quiz.explanation: Most vegetables need about 5 mm per day in dry conditions.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a filter in a sprinkler system?
quiz.explanation: Filters remove debris that can clog sprinkler nozzles.

quiz.q: Which pipe size is commonly used for mainlines in small portable systems?
quiz.explanation: 32-40 mm HDPE is typical for mainlines to reduce friction loss.

quiz.q: What is a quick-connect coupler used for?
quiz.explanation: Quick-connect couplers allow fast assembly and disassembly of pipes.

quiz.q: How can you reduce application rate if it causes runoff?
quiz.explanation: Smaller nozzles reduce flow, lowering application rate.

quiz.q: What is the recommended overlap for sprinkler spacing?
quiz.explanation: At least 30% overlap ensures uniform coverage without dry spots.

quiz.q: What should you do before connecting sprinklers to a new system?
options: D) Run pump for an hour
quiz.explanation: Flushing removes debris that could clog sprinklers.

quiz.q: How often should you check sprinkler nozzles for clogs?
options: B) Every time you move them
quiz.explanation: Regular checks prevent uneven watering and keep the system efficient.

quiz.q: What is a good way to check actual application depth?
quiz.explanation: Placing tin cans around the plot and measuring water depth gives actual application.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid lifting pipes when moving them?
quiz.explanation: Dragging pipes prevents cracks and kinks; lifting can cause damage.

quiz.q: In highland areas with frost, what should you do to pipes before storage?
quiz.explanation: Draining prevents freezing and bursting.

quiz.q: How should you clean micro-sprinklers with mineral deposits?
quiz.explanation: Vinegar dissolves mineral deposits without damaging plastic.

quiz.q: Where should you store plastic pipes?
options: C) In a shaded, dry place
quiz.explanation: UV light degrades plastic, so store in shade and dry conditions.

quiz.q: What should you lubricate on an impact sprinkler?
quiz.explanation: A drop of oil on the bearing keeps it rotating smoothly.

quiz.q: If a sprinkler doesnât rotate, what is a likely cause?
quiz.explanation: Dirt or damage in the bearing prevents rotation.

quiz.q: What should you do if pressure is low at the sprinkler?
quiz.explanation: A clogged filter restricts flow and reduces pressure.

quiz.q: How can you temporarily fix a cracked pipe?
quiz.explanation: Self-amalgamating tape provides a quick, watertight seal.

quiz.q: What causes runoff in a sprinkler system?
options: A) Application rate higher than soil intake
quiz.explanation: If water is applied faster than soil can absorb, runoff occurs.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool to keep in your sprinkler repair kit?
quiz.explanation: Spare gaskets fix leaks at couplers quickly.

quiz.q: Why is it important to mark sprinkler positions?
options: A) To save time when moving
quiz.explanation: Marking positions avoids re-measuring each time you move the system.

quiz.q: What is a 'two-line' system?
options: B) One lateral watering while another is moved
quiz.explanation: A two-line system keeps water application continuous by alternating laterals.

quiz.q: How can wind affect sprinkler uniformity?
quiz.explanation: Wind blows spray off-target, leading to dry spots and overwatering.

quiz.q: What should you do if a sprinkler sprays from its base?
quiz.explanation: A bad seal at the base causes leakage; replace it.

quiz.q: How long can a well-stored sprinkler system last?
quiz.explanation: With proper storage and maintenance, systems last 5-10 years.

quiz.q: What is the first step when troubleshooting uneven coverage?
quiz.explanation: Pressure is the most common cause of uneven coverage; check it first.
